<reason>A won the narrow-exception clash. It directly answered the pressure questions, excluded preliminary stays and routine incomplete-record cases, and distinguished necessary investigation from ordinary research value. B defended consent and community authority forcefully, but repeatedly claimed every incomplete file would justify delay without overcoming A's stricter conditions. Its proposed evidence substitutes also failed to answer the otherwise-unrecoverable evidence scenario. A's comparison of bounded, externally authorized delay with permanent evidentiary loss was ultimately more persuasive than B's categorical priority for immediate return.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>After B accepted immediate return even when examination was necessary to preserve otherwise-lost evidence, A showed why archives and later authorized study could not resolve that case. Combined with its concrete example of a routine teaching collection that would fail the necessity test, this substantially weakened B's portrayal of the exception as ordinary research detention.</best_rebuttal>
